answers.q: Under Article 6 of the AI Act, when is an AI system classified as high-risk?
answers.answer: An AI system is classified as high‑risk when (i) it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product or is itself a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, **and** the product or AI system must undergo a third‑party conformity assessment under that legislation [2]; and (ii) any AI system listed in Annex III is also deemed high‑risk, unless it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons [2].

answers.q: What transparency obligations does Article 50 of the AI Act impose?
answers.answer:
Article 50 creates several transparency duties for providers and deployers of AI systems that generate or manipulate content:

* Providers must ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons inform those persons that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious to a reasonably well‑informed, observant and circumspect user [2].  
* Providers of systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text must mark the outputs in a machine‑readable format so that they can be detected as artificially generated or manipulated, using technical solutions that are effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible [2].  
* Deployers of AI systems that produce deep‑fake image, audio or video must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated, except where the use is authorised by law for criminal‑justice purposes; for artistic, satirical or fictional works the disclosure may be limited to a non‑intrusive notice [4].  
* Deployers who publish AI‑generated text on matters of public interest must also disclose its artificial origin, unless the content has undergone human editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility [4].  
* The information about AI‑generated content must be presented to the natural persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of first interaction or exposure and must meet applicable accessibility requirements [1].  
* These obligations do not affect other transparency requirements set out elsewhere in the Regulation or in Union or national law [1].

answers.q: What right does Article 17 of the GDPR create?
answers.answer: Article 17 of the GDPR creates a “right to erasure” (the “right to be forgotten”), whereby the data subject may obtain from the controller the deletion of personal data concerning them without undue delay when one of the listed grounds applies【6】.
citations: Data Protection Act 2018 (Section 60(4)) (Data Protection Commission) Regulations 2025.

answers.q: What lawful bases for processing are listed in Article 6 of the GDPR?
What does Article 33 of the GDPR require after a personal data breach?
answers.answer:
The controller must notify the competent supervisory authority “without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it”, unless the breach is unlikely to risk the rights and freedoms of natural persons; if the notification is later than 72 hours, reasons for the delay must be given【2】.  
The notification must at least (a) describe the nature of the breach, including where possible the categories and approximate number of data subjects and records concerned, (b) provide the name and contact details of the data‑protection officer or other contact point, (c) describe the likely consequences of the breach, and (d) describe the measures taken or proposed to address it and mitigate adverse effects【2】.  
The processor must inform the controller “without undue delay” after becoming aware of the breach【2】.  
The controller must also document the breach – the facts, effects and remedial action – so that the supervisory authority can verify compliance【7】.

answers.q: What does section 4 of the Immigration Act 2004 say about permission to land?
answers.answer:
Section 4 of the Immigration Act 2004 provides that an immigration officer, on behalf of the Minister, may give a non‑national a document or place an inscription on his or her passport (or other equivalent document) authorising the person to land or remain in the State [1].  
A non‑national arriving by air or sea from outside the State must present himself or herself to an immigration officer on arrival and apply for a permission [1].  
The officer may refuse permission if satisfied that the person (a) cannot support himself or any dependants, (b) intends to take employment without a valid employment permit, (c) suffers from a condition listed in the First Schedule, (d) has been convicted of an offence punishable by imprisonment of one year or more, or (e) is not exempt under an order made under section 17 [1].  
The permission may include conditions (e.g., duration of stay, engagement in employment, business or a profession) which the Minister may amend, and the non‑national must comply with those conditions [7].  
A permission may be renewed or varied by the Minister or an immigration officer on the Minister’s behalf upon application by the non‑national [7].

answers.q: What does section 3 of the Immigration Act 1999 provide about deportation orders?
answers.answer: Section 3 of the Immigration Act 1999 allows the Minister to issue a deportation order requiring any non‑national named in the order to leave the State within a period specified in the order and to remain outside the State thereafter, subject to the prohibition of refoulement under the Refugee Act 1996 and the other provisions of section 3【7】. The section also lists the categories of persons for whom such an order may be made, including those who have served a prison term, those whose deportation has been recommended by a court, persons subject to certain European Community regulations, and persons whose asylum applications have been refused or transferred, among others【7】.

answers.q: What does Article 7 of the Free Movement Directive say about the right of residence for more than three months?
answers.answer: Article 7 (1) of Directive 2004/38/EC provides that a Union citizen has the right of residence in another Member State for a period longer than three months if they (a) are a worker or self‑employed person in the host Member State; or (b) have sufficient resources for themselves and their family members so as not to become a burden on the host State’s social assistance system and have comprehensive sickness‑insurance cover in that State; or (c) are enrolled at a private or public establishment accredited or financed by the host Member State on the basis of … [6]

answers.q: What does Article 35 of the Free Movement Directive say about abuse of rights and marriages of convenience?
answers.answer: Article 35 of Directive 2004/38 permits Member States to adopt the necessary measures to refuse, terminate or withdraw any right conferred by the Directive in cases of abuse of rights or fraud, such as marriages of convenience, and any such measure must be proportionate and subject to the procedural safeguards provided for in Articles 30 and 31 [1][4][7].

answers.q: What does Article 8 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights protect?
answers.answer: Article 8 of the Charter protects the right of everyone to the protection of personal data concerning them, requiring that such data be processed fairly, for specified purposes and on a lawful basis, and guaranteeing rights of access and rectification, with oversight by an independent authority【7】.

answers.q: What does Article 15 of the ePrivacy Directive allow Member States to do?
answers.answer: Article 15 permits Member States to adopt legislative measures that restrict the scope of the rights and obligations set out in Articles 5, 6, 8(1‑4) and 9 of the ePrivacy Directive where such restriction is a necessary, appropriate and proportionate measure within a democratic society to safeguard national security (state security), defence, public security, or the prevention, investigation, detection and prosecution of criminal offences or unauthorised use of the electronic communications system; it also allows them to introduce limited‑period data‑retention measures, provided the measures comply with the general principles of Community law, including those in Article 6(1‑2) of the Treaty on European Union【5†L1-L5】.

answers.q: What does Article 4 of the DSM Copyright Directive provide about text and data mining?
answers.answer:
Article 4 creates a specific exception or limitation for text‑and‑data‑mining:  

1. Member States must allow reproductions and extractions of lawfully accessible works or other subject‑matter for the purposes of text‑and‑data‑mining (Article 5(a) and Article 7(1) of Directive 96/9/EC, Article 2 of Directive 2001/29/EC, Article 4(1)(a) & (b) of Directive 2009/24/EC and Article 15(1) of this Directive) [4].  

2. Copies made under that exception may be kept for as long as necessary for the text‑and‑data‑mining purpose [4].  

3. The exception does not apply if the rightholder has expressly reserved the right to prohibit such reproductions or extractions, for example by using machine‑readable notices for content made publicly available online [4].  

4. Article 4 does not affect the operation of Article 3 of the Directive [4].

answers.q: What conditions does the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956 set for a certificate of naturalisation?
answers.answer:
The Act sets that a certificate of naturalisation may be revoked if the Minister is satisfied that any of the conditions in section 19(1) apply, namely:  

* the certificate was obtained by fraud, mis‑representation (whether innocent or fraudulent) or concealment of material facts or circumstances; [1]  
* the person, by an overt act, has failed in his duty of fidelity to the nation and loyalty to the State; [1]  
* the person is not of Irish descent or associations and has been ordinarily resident outside the State (or, for a section 15A naturalisation, outside the island of Ireland otherwise than in the public service) for a continuous period of seven years without reasonable excuse and has not annually registered his name and a declaration of intention to retain Irish citizenship with an Irish diplomatic mission, consular office or the Minister. [1]  

The Act also allows the Minister, under section 16, to dispense with the normal naturalisation conditions in certain cases, such as where the applicant is of Irish descent or associations, is a parent or guardian of a minor of Irish descent, is a naturalised citizen acting for a minor child, is married to a naturalised or Irish citizen, or is or has been resident abroad in the public service. [7]
citations: Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956 (Revocation of Certificate of Naturalisation) (Prescribed Forms) Regulations 2025.

answers.q: How long does a controller have to notify a personal data breach to the supervisory authority?
answers.answer: A controller must notify the supervisory authority “without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of” the breach, unless the breach is unlikely to pose a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons【1†L1-L3】【2†L1-L3】【5†L1-L3】.

answers.q: What is the maximum administrative fine under the GDPR?
answers.answer: The GDPR provides for administrative fines of up to 20 000 000 EUR, or, for an undertaking, up to 4 % of its total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [2].
citations: Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Act 2026, s. 105
Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Act 2026, s. 105

answers.q: What are the maximum penalties under the AI Act for engaging in a prohibited AI practice?
answers.answer: Non‑compliance with a prohibited AI practice under Article 5 can be punished with administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000, or, for an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher【5】.

answers.q: How long may an EU citizen reside in another Member State without any conditions or formalities?
answers.answer: An EU citizen may reside in another Member State for up to three months without any conditions or formalities other than holding a valid identity card or passport【1】.

answers.q: What is the maximum fine a very large online platform can face under the Digital Services Act?
answers.answer: The Commission may impose fines of up to 6 % of the provider’s total worldwide annual turnover in the preceding financial year for infringements of the Regulation [6].

answers.q: What are the time limits for a transfer under the Dublin III Regulation?
answers.answer:
The Dublin III Regulation sets a general deadline of **six months** from the moment the request is accepted (or from the final decision on an appeal or review with suspensive effect) for the transfer to be carried out [3]. If the transfer is delayed beyond six months, the responsible Member State is relieved of its obligations and the request passes back to the requesting Member State; the deadline may be extended to a maximum of **one year** where the person is imprisoned, or to **eighteen months** where the person absconds [1].  

When a person is detained for the purpose of transfer, the transfer must occur **as soon as practically possible and at the latest within six weeks** of the acceptance of the request or the end of any suspensive effect [5].
citations: Asylum and Migration Management Regulation, Article 46

answers.q: How many years of reckonable residence are needed to apply for Irish naturalisation?
answers.answer: Five years of reckonable residence are required for an adult applicant to be eligible for Irish naturalisation【1】【3】【4】.

answers.q: What turnover and user thresholds make an undertaking a gatekeeper under the Digital Markets Act?
answers.answer:
An undertaking is presumed to be a gatekeeper when it meets the quantitative thresholds set out in Article 3 (2) of the DMA:  

* an annual Union turnover of **at least EUR 7.5 billion** in each of the last three financial years, **or** an average market‑capitalisation/equivalent fair market value of **at least EUR 75 billion** in the last financial year, together with provision of the same core platform service in at least three Member States; and  
* in the last financial year it has **at least 45 million monthly active end users** established or located in the Union **and** **at least 10 000 yearly active business users** established in the Union [2].

answers.q: Can the non-EEA spouse of an EU citizen working in Ireland be refused residence because they never lawfully lived in the EU before?
answers.answer: No. A non‑EEA spouse of an EU‑citizen who is exercising Treaty rights in Ireland can be granted a residence card even if that spouse has never previously lived lawfully in another EU Member State. The rules apply to family members of an EU‑citizen who are residing with that citizen in Ireland, not to any prior residence history [4]. If the EU‑citizen is exercising a Treaty right (e.g., working, self‑employed, studying or self‑sufficient) the non‑EEA spouse is a “qualifying family member” and may be issued a Residence Card of a Family Member of a Union Citizen (Stamp 4 EU‑FAM) [3].

answers.q: Does a third-country national parent of a dependent EU-citizen child have a right to reside in the EU?
answers.answer: A third‑country‑national parent who is the primary carer of a minor child who is an EU citizen may be granted a derived right of residence in the host Member State, because refusing that parent residence would deprive the child of the genuine enjoyment of its Union‑citizen right of residence and would compel the child to leave the EU [1][6].

answers.q: Is a same-sex spouse a spouse for the purposes of EU free movement rights?
answers.answer: Yes. The Court has held that the term “spouse” in Article 2(2)(a) of Directive 2004/38 is gender‑neutral and therefore includes a same‑sex spouse of an EU citizen [4][8]. This interpretation obliges Member States to recognise such marriages for the purpose of granting the derived right of residence, even if the State does not provide for same‑sex marriage in its own law [5].

answers.q: Why did the Court of Justice invalidate the Safe Harbour decision on transfers to the United States?
answers.answer: The Court found that Decision 2000/520 (the Safe Harbour) did not provide a level of protection “essentially equivalent to that guaranteed in the EU legal order” and therefore failed to meet the adequacy requirement of Article 25(6) of Directive 95/46, read in the light of the Charter [2]. It concluded that the decision could not comply with the substantive Safe Harbour principles and the national‑security exemption, because the United States did not ensure an adequate level of protection and the decision lacked effective safeguards and redress mechanisms for data subjects [1][5][6]. Consequently, the Safe Harbour regime was declared invalid.

answers.q: Why was the EU-US Privacy Shield held invalid?
answers.answer: The Court held that the EU‑U.S. Privacy Shield was incompatible with the GDPR because Article 1 of the Decision, which declared that the United States ensures an adequate level of protection, conflicted with Article 45(1) of the GDPR when read in light of Charter articles 7, 8 and 47; consequently the whole Decision was declared invalid [3][7]. The Court’s final judgment formally annulled Decision (EU) 2016/1250, finding the adequacy decision invalid [2].

answers.q: Must a search engine remove links to personal data when the person asks?
answers.answer: Yes. Under Article 12(b) and sub‑paragraph (a) of the first paragraph of Article 14 of Directive 95/46, a data subject may require the operator of a search engine to remove from the list of results links to web pages that contain personal information about him, even where that information has not been erased from the original pages and even if its publication on those pages is lawful【1†L1-L4】【7†L1-L4】.

answers.q: What must a provider of a high-risk AI system do before placing it on the market?
answers.answer: Before placing a high‑risk AI system on the market, the provider must ensure that the system bears the required CE marking, is accompanied by a copy of the EU declaration of conformity and the appropriate instructions for use, and that the provider (and, where applicable, the importer) has complied with its obligations under Article 16 (b) and (c) and Article 23(3) [4]. The provider must also make the system’s characteristics, capabilities, limitations and any known or foreseeable risks transparent to deployers, as required for high‑risk AI systems [3].

answers.q: When is a general-purpose AI model considered to carry systemic risk?
answers.answer: A general‑purpose AI model is regarded as presenting systemic risk when it has high‑impact capabilities – i.e., capabilities that match or exceed those of the most advanced general‑purpose AI models and that could have a significant impact on the internal market because of its reach [1]. If the model meets the applicable threshold for such high‑impact capabilities, it is presumed to be a general‑purpose AI model with systemic risk and the provider must notify the AI Office within two weeks of meeting the requirements or becoming aware that the model will meet them [2].

answers.q: How does the law treat AI used to infer emotions of employees at work?
answers.answer: The AI Act prohibits the placing on the market, putting into service or use of AI systems that identify or infer emotions or intentions of natural persons on the basis of biometric data in situations related to the workplace, because such systems can lead to discriminatory outcomes and intrude on fundamental rights [1]. This prohibition does not apply to systems placed on the market strictly for medical or safety reasons [1]. The regulation also defines an “emotion‑recognition system” as an AI system for identifying or inferring emotions such as happiness, sadness, anger, etc., on the basis of biometric data [3].

answers.q: What happens to a family member's right of residence if the EU citizen they depend on dies or leaves?
answers.answer:
If the Union (EU/EEA/Swiss) citizen dies, a family member who was already exercising a right of residence in Ireland retains that right provided they had been residing with the Union citizen for at least one year before the death [2]. The surviving family member may continue to reside on an individual, personal basis.  

If the Union citizen leaves Ireland, the family member who is not a Member‑State national may keep the right of residence they enjoyed at the time of the departure, provided they have been residing in Ireland as a family member for at least one year [2].  

Where the Union citizen had already acquired a right of permanent residence (continuous residence of at least two years) and the family member was employed or self‑employed in Ireland, the family member may also remain permanently after the citizen’s death [6][7].  

If the surviving family member is a parent with custody of a child who was enrolled in an Irish educational establishment, that parent may reside until the child completes the course of study, regardless of the parent’s nationality [2].
citations: European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) (No. 2) Regulations 2006
European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) Regulations 2006

answers.q: What is subsidiary protection and who qualifies for it?
answers.answer:
Subsidiary protection is a form of international protection that recognises a third‑country national or a stateless person as a “person eligible for subsidiary protection” and confers “subsidiary protection status” on that person [3][4].  

A person is eligible for subsidiary protection when they do not qualify as a refugee but “substantial grounds have been shown for believing… that… if returned to his or her country of origin (or, for a stateless person, to his or her country of former habitual residence), they would face a real risk of suffering serious harm” and they are unable or, owing to that risk, unwilling to avail themselves of the protection of that country [2][3].

answers.q: On what grounds does the Equal Status Act prohibit discrimination?
answers.answer: The Equal Status Act 2000 prohibits discrimination on the following grounds: gender, marital status, family status, sexual orientation, religion (or belief), age (subject to subsection 3), disability, race/colour/nationality or ethnic or national origins, and membership of the Traveller community【7】.

answers.q: How must Irish courts interpret legislation in light of the European Convention on Human Rights?
answers.answer: Irish courts must give judicial notice to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms and, when interpreting and applying its provisions, must take due account of the principles laid down in any declaration, decision, advisory opinion or judgment of the European Court of Human Rights (or related bodies) [1].  In doing so, “the Convention” is understood as the text set out in Schedule 1 of the Act, as amended by the relevant protocols, and courts must interpret legislation in accordance with those Convention provisions, subject to any derogation under Article 15 [5].
citations: European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003, s. 4
